# Force Based Gamemastering #

### A guide to help you run reactive non-linear campaigns ###

## Introduction: Why This Guide Exists ##

### Why I'm Writing This ###

Much of the campaign-creation advice I've encountered seems to lead to campaigns that feel dead to me: either the game is pushed along a predetermined track, or the GM is left stranded when the characters do something nobody could have predicted. I want enough understanding of the situation to respond in real time without predicting what the characters will do.

My approach starts with a theme: a question or idea the campaign keeps putting into play. I build a Stage of places, histories, relationships, and pressures, then add Forces—people or groups pursuing goals within their limits. Their collisions create situations and fallout the characters can engage with. Together, these parts let the campaign explore its theme from different angles without deciding what the characters must believe or how the question should be answered.

I invest heavily in the initial campaign, then prepare less between sessions. That first work gives me a model of the situation, not a sequence of events. At the table, I follow what the characters do and use the established world to respond. When deciding what happens next, my first question is, “What is the most interesting outcome that can happen within the theme?” Then I work out how that outcome can grow from the established situation. Theme leads what I look for; it does not authorize me to force an unsupported consequence or steer the players toward an answer. The aim is for the world to surprise us without feeling arbitrary.

### What This Guide Will—and Won't—Teach ###

This is a style of play built around a substantial initial investment and low-maintenance preparation afterward. It is meant to help a GM follow the joy of the table and improvise freely, while giving them enough understanding to keep the campaign feeling cohesive.

It is not a formula for producing a successful campaign. The ideas here are rules of thumb, not laws. They can—and should—be changed to fit the circumstances, and understanding why a rule of thumb exists matters more than following it mechanically. This approach cannot guarantee that a game will be fun, remove the GM's responsibility for story design, or prevent every improvised choice from disrupting continuity or even breaking the story. It offers tools that can help prevent those problems and help a GM respond when the unexpected happens.

### Who This Approach Might Suit ###

I'm writing this first to capture my own thoughts so I can review and refine them. Eventually, I hope to publish the guide freely on the web. I especially hope it will help new Gamemasters, and that some of its techniques will inspire the people writing books about running games.

This approach may suit a GM who enjoys responding to players more than steering them toward a planned sequence, but still wants the world to feel consistent. It may also suit someone willing to spend time developing a campaign before play in exchange for having less to prepare between sessions. It won't be the right fit for every GM or every table; the point is to understand the approach well enough to decide what is useful for yours.

### How to Use This Guide ###

Skim the guide first to get a sense of the whole approach, then read more deeply wherever a chapter is useful to you. You don't need to adopt every rule of thumb. As you read, consider why I use each one, what it is meant to accomplish, and what might need to change for your group.

If you are new to the approach, the parts follow a progression: Part I explains my aims and principles; Part II develops the starting situation and preparation; Part III covers play at the table; Part IV covers sessions, campaigns, and problems; and Part V offers an example and ways to adapt the approach. Details such as starting with three forces, my preparation ratios, and opening with combat are preferences and rules of thumb, not requirements.

The examples show what these ideas have looked like in my games, not what every campaign should look like. I always begin with combat created by the collision of forces' actions. The characters may be caught in the fallout rather than fighting those forces directly. That is one way I put the campaign in motion; the larger principle is to create a situation with energy and connections, then let play determine what happens next.

### 1. What a Good Game Looks Like to Me ###

#### What I Want Players to Experience ####

I want the game to feel like a good carnival ride: adrenaline, exhaustion, excitement, and real emotion. I want everyone at the table to have a good time.

My biggest sign that a game has worked is what the players do when it ends. Either they don't want to leave, or they leave rehashing what happened. That energy—the desire to stay in the experience or to keep talking about it afterward—is what I look for.

##### I Design Systems, Not Stories #####

In this guide, a **Force** is a person or group with a goal and enough power in a relevant arena to affect the situation. Chapter 5 develops the full criteria, including the limits and fingerprint that help make a Force useful in play.

I build a world with enough pressure and meaning for the players' choices, the forces' actions, and the Stage's tensions to create the story in play.

#### What Makes a Session Feel Successful ####

A session is successful when the players are engaged enough to want more, or when the events keep mattering to them afterward. It can feel cohesive even when the characters surprise me and change the situation.

#### What I Prioritize When I Can't Have Everything ####

The table's fun is the only thing I will not sacrifice. Everything else can give way: the plot, the characters, the NPCs, the current TTRPG system, and more.

If the dice are getting in the way, I throw them out and play make-believe instead. Whatever works for the table is more important than continuing to use a rule or tool that is making the game less fun.

#### What I'm Comfortable Leaving Out ####

I'm comfortable leaving out or changing anything that gets in the way of the table's fun. I don't need to preserve a planned plot, protect an NPC from the consequences of play, or keep using a system just because we started with it.

This doesn't mean I don't care about continuity, characters, or the story. I use preparation and the campaign's forces to help keep events coherent while improvising. But those are ways to support the experience, not obligations that outrank it.

### 2. The GM's Job—and Its Limits ###

#### What I Take Responsibility For ####

I technically have authority over the forces and the world's reactions, but I don't think of myself as standing above the table. I think of myself as its steward. My job is to help create and maintain a situation the table can enjoy, and to respond to what happens without forcing the game down a predetermined path.

That includes making calls in the moment. I use the forces, their goals and limits, and what has already happened to make the world's responses feel like they belong. I also take responsibility for making the game safe enough for everyone at the table to participate.

#### What I Leave to the Players ####

I don't try to predict what the characters will do or require them to follow a planned sequence. The players decide what their characters attempt, and those choices can change the campaign.

#### What We Decide Together ####

Safety is the ultimate authority at my table. As a group, we decide what can initially go into the game and when it can happen. During play, every player has veto power over content, no questions asked. This is my one hard rule.

When someone uses a veto, the offending context is removed. The practical steps I use to establish and honor this boundary are in Chapter 4.

The table's fun is shared, too. I am a member of the table, and my enjoyment matters as much as any one player's. I find enjoyment in doing something well, so I'm willing to throw out the plot, characters, NPCs, or even the system if that is what the table needs. I recommend that prospective GMs figure out what makes GMing enjoyable for them and find a group that wants that kind of game. I usually ask my players to help us find our fun together. If we can't, I end the game; if one person at the table isn't having fun, it tends to tank the whole table.

#### How Authority Works at My Table ####

My authority over the forces and the world's reactions is practical, not absolute. I use it in service of the table, never to overrule a safety veto or protect a planned story. If there is a conflict about a rule or ruling, I bring it to a table vote and move on. My approach to ordinary rules questions is covered in [Making Decisions in the Moment](#8-making-decisions-in-the-moment).

### 3. The Principles Behind My Decisions ###

#### My Core Principles ####

##### Safety is the hard boundary #####

The table decides what content is acceptable, and every player can veto content at any time without explanation. Nothing about a plot, encounter, or character takes priority over that.

##### The table's fun comes first #####

The table's fun is the one thing I will not sacrifice. Plot, characters, NPCs, and even the game system are all things I can change or discard if they get in the way. I am part of the table, too, so I look for a kind of play we can enjoy together.

##### Theme gives the campaign meaning #####

Theme is the question or idea the campaign keeps putting into play. I develop the Stage, Forces, their collisions, and the fallout so that, together, they let the characters encounter it from different angles. When deciding what happens next, I first ask, “What is the most interesting outcome that can happen within the theme?” Then I work out how the established situation can bring it about. No single detail has to represent the theme; the campaign's parts create opportunities to explore it through play. The characters' choices let us see what the question means to them. I do not use theme to dictate a lesson or decide the answer. Safety, the table's fun, and the players' freedom to choose remain essential.

##### Prepare situations, not outcomes #####

I put substantial effort into the initial campaign concepts, especially the forces: what they want, what they will and will not do, and how their actions can be recognized. I use this preparation to understand the situation, not to predict what the characters will do or dictate what must happen.

Theme guides that preparation by giving it a question to explore. I use it to shape the Stage, the forces and their goals, their fingerprints, and the conflicts their actions create, so their details work together to raise that question in play. It does not prescribe what the characters must do or believe.

##### Let play change the situation #####

The characters' actions matter. Forces pursue their goals, react to interference, and may change as the campaign develops. I follow what the table finds engaging rather than insisting that players pursue every prepared thread.

##### Preserve the Appearance of Continuity #####

Continuity is not important for its own sake; what matters is its appearance. I want events and character actions to fit the players' understanding of the world and its theme, so that changes do not break that understanding or make the campaign's meaning feel arbitrary. I can engineer an explanation backward when needed. Often the players will make those connections for me, filling in how a new development fits what they already know.

There is a kind of magic in this. Players can experience the world as solid and complete, and the GM as an extraordinary planner, even when the GM is improvising. The goal is not to fool the players about what was prepared in advance. Like a magician creating a moment of wonder, I want us to share an experience that feels magical and memorable. The preparation gives me enough understanding to respond coherently; play supplies the unexpected connections.

##### Treat the GM as a steward #####

I technically decide how forces and the world react, but I think of myself as the table's steward, not as an authority standing outside it. My decisions should help the group have a good experience, not protect my plans from the players.

#### How These Principles Affect Play ####

I prefer encounters to arise from the fallout of character actions rather than being inserted as separate events. In tactical games, I prepare spreads of enemies for different encounter types and reskin them to fit the situation that actually arises.

#### When Principles Conflict ####

Safety is the hard boundary; within it, the table's fun comes first. Continuity helps players trust the world, but I will revise details rather than let literal consistency undermine player choice or enjoyment.

#### Where My Approach Differs from Familiar Advice ####

The advice I have the biggest problem with is advice that starts by having the GM create encounters as separate units. Encounters are important, but I find they work better when they flow naturally from the fallout of character actions. That way, the encounter belongs to the developing situation instead of interrupting it.

This is more difficult in tactical games such as D&D, where encounters may need carefully composed enemy groups. Preparing adaptable enemy spreads lets me keep that tactical structure without deciding in advance when or why an encounter will occur.

### 4. Finding the Right Fit ###

#### Choosing a System for the Experience I Want ####

For me, the system is almost inconsequential. You can tell any kind of story with any kind of system. What matters most is that the table will have fun with the system; everything after that can be patched.

That does not mean system choice is meaningless. I recommend that GMs understand what they like and dislike. I personally don't run tactical systems anymore because I don't find them fun. I prefer story-based systems, so I tend to run games such as World of Darkness, Fate, and Cypher. Those are my tastes, not a universal recommendation. Choose a system the table wants to play, then adapt what needs adapting.

#### Finding Players Who Want That Experience ####

I am up front with players about the kind of game I expect to run. I may not reveal the exact theme if doing so would give too much away, but I talk about what kinds of things will be in the story and what parts of play are likely to take focus: combat, narrative, investigation, or some combination.

I also tell players what topics I want to address, especially when those topics might be trigger topics. Players need enough information to decide whether they want to join, even when some details of the story remain a surprise.

#### Establishing Expectations, Boundaries, and Feedback ####

Before play, we decide together what content can go into the game and when it can happen. Every player can veto content at any time, no questions asked. If a veto is used, I remove the offending context, make a note, and after the session ask only whether I recorded it correctly so it can be added to our banned-topics list.

##### Why the Veto Is Needed #####

The veto protects a player's agency and consent during play. Agreeing to join a game, or agreeing beforehand that a topic is acceptable, does not mean agreeing to endure every way that topic might unfold. The player has the final say over whether they continue engaging with content that affects them.

Nobody can be completely self-aware all the time. A player may discover a boundary only when something in play affects them. They may not understand their reaction yet, much less be able to explain it. They do not need to have identified or announced that boundary beforehand for it to matter.

Things happen quickly at the table, and we sometimes respond by instinct. An interaction or improvised detail can accidentally trigger someone even when everyone is acting with care. The veto is not a judgment that the GM was careless or that a player failed to disclose something. Nobody has to have failed for it to be needed.

It is an escape valve: a way out of that moment and back toward normalcy at the table. An agreed list of banned topics is useful, but it cannot anticipate everything that might affect someone. The veto remains available when a reaction surprises everyone, including the person experiencing it.

"Stop this" is sufficient. The player does not need to understand their reaction, disclose personal experiences, provide proof, defend a boundary, or negotiate for permission. A veto is not debated or put to a vote. I remove the offending context and its direct consequences. If the veto concerns an action by a player character, I work with that player to find another action the character can take. The fiction can change; the person should not have to endure the moment for the game to continue.

##### Why We Practice Before Play #####

I don't start a game with a player until we have practiced vetoing topics twice. The first practice is usually silly: I might say, “Ham is your trigger topic and bread is yours,” then describe a scene that includes one of those topics so everyone can try using a veto. I repeat the exercise with a different, real example, such as animal abuse, if it is not already on the forbidden-topics list.

Knowing that a veto is allowed is different from feeling able to use it in a fast-moving or emotionally intense moment. Practice makes it a familiar, available action before someone discovers they need it. Each player gets to rehearse using the veto and experience the table honoring it. I also get to practice stopping and removing the context promptly, without asking for an explanation or turning it into a discussion.

The purpose is to rehearse the procedure, not to test anyone's limits or require personal disclosure. I want using the escape valve to take as little effort as possible when a real moment calls for it.

##### When Practice Feels Infantilizing #####

Some players may find this practice patronizing, especially the silly example. They are adults who understand what "stop" means, and being asked to demonstrate it can feel as though I doubt their competence or am treating them like children. That is a concern worth taking seriously, not evidence that they disregard safety or consent.

Understanding the rule is not what we are practicing. A player can understand it perfectly and still hesitate to interrupt a scene everyone else seems to enjoy, abandon something the GM has prepared, or act on a reaction they cannot yet explain. Experience does not make someone immune to those pressures. Practice gives them a chance to see that using the veto really does stop the content without requiring a defense. It gives them evidence of how this table responds, rather than only my promise about how it will respond.

The rest of us are practicing too. I rehearse stopping and removing the context; everyone else rehearses accepting the interruption without debating it, demanding reasons, or making the person responsible for restoring the mood. The player using the veto is not performing for my approval. We are rehearsing a shared procedure in which that player's decision is sufficient.

Many people have experienced the same reason for rehearsal in workplace safety drills, especially in jobs with specialized safety concerns. Competent adults practice so that an unexpected, stressful moment is not their first attempt at using the procedure, and so everyone knows how to respond when someone signals a problem. The comparison is about why we rehearse, not about equating a game with a hazardous workplace. A drill can itself be patronizing or perfunctory; the analogy does not excuse that here.

That distinction matters. Infantilization would mean treating players as incapable of understanding or managing their own experience and substituting my judgment for theirs. The veto does the opposite: I cannot know their experience for them, so they retain the authority to stop content even when I do not understand why. Practice is meant to make that authority usable, not to assess their maturity.

A worthwhile purpose does not excuse a patronizing presentation. I explain the reason before the exercise, keep it brief, and take part myself rather than adopting the role of a teacher testing students. If the silly example feels demeaning, we can choose a straightforward, low-stakes example instead. The silliness is not the point; rehearsing both the veto and the table's response is.

I might introduce it this way:

> We are not practicing because I think you do not understand the word "stop." We are practicing so you can see what happens when you use it, and so all of us, including me, rehearse responding without making you explain yourself. I do not want the first time we try this together to be a moment when someone actually needs it.

If someone objects, I ask what about the exercise feels patronizing and discuss its format rather than treating the objection as proof that they need instruction. I still require practice before play at my table, but I do not need to insist on a particular performance or joke to accomplish it. The aim is to establish a trustworthy response together, not to demand that players prove they can follow directions.

### 5. Creating a Starting Point ###

#### What I Need to Know Before Play Begins ####

I think of campaign creation as building a physics engine: create a situation with Forces that can move the world, then let the characters enter and change what happens. I need to understand the situation well enough to respond to surprises, not know what story the players will produce. The Stage gives Forces a world to act in; collisions between them start Arcs that develop through play.

##### Begin with a Theme #####

Before I develop the campaign, I decide what it is about. I call that its theme: a question, such as “Can you hunt monsters without becoming one?”, or an idea I want to explore. A question opens up possibilities rather than supplying an answer; the campaign's situations give players chances to explore what it means to their characters.

What makes a theme good for this approach is not how clever or open-ended its wording sounds, but whether this GM and these players can keep interacting with it. A fruitful theme keeps giving the GM ways to create situations around it and gives the players ways to explore it through their characters' choices. It does not run out after one dilemma or one obvious answer; the changing campaign can bring it forward from new angles. “Good versus evil” may feel settled and offer little to a particular group, but for a group that wants to question what good and evil mean, it can sustain rich play. The right theme depends on what the people at the table find meaningful to explore.

Theme is not a label I attach after creation. It guides how I develop the Stage, Forces, their goals and fingerprints, their collisions, and their fallout, so the whole situation raises the question from different angles. No single detail needs to represent the theme, and no Force needs to stand for one side of an argument. I create varied pressures for the characters to encounter; the players decide what those pressures mean and how to respond.

In a Mage: The Ascension game, my theme was “Can you hunt monsters without becoming one?” I populated the city with a monstrous but not evil Sabbat pack and bishop, a cold and calculating Nosferatu Camarilla prince, a cold war between the two, two different vampire Anarch groups, a werewolf civil war, and a history of vampires mysteriously losing key leaders. No one detail was the theme. Together, they gave “monster” more than one meaning and made the question part of the city rather than a speech the characters had to hear.

The starting forces were an Anarch leader who wanted vampires revealed to the world so it would become a world where only the strong survive; a prince in danger of being removed by the Camarilla because he had only become prince after his predecessor disappeared; and an overworked, understaffed police force fighting to prevent further defunding. The starting collision came from the Anarchs wanting to forcibly recruit a police detective while the Sabbat wanted to kill him. The detective smelled something fishy and sent the characters to investigate. They found themselves between two overwhelming vampire forces, neither interested in fighting them. The opening offered one way into the campaign's question; the wider city and the characters' choices would keep exploring it without deciding what they should do or conclude about the monsters around them.

##### Forces #####

At its core, a Force is a person or group with a goal and more power than the characters in the arena where it pursues that goal, giving it the ability to move the world. A Force is not the same thing as an antagonist: "Force" describes an actor's capacity to affect the situation, while "antagonist" describes its relationship to the characters or their aims. A Force might help the characters, oppose them, or pursue goals that have little to do with them. That relationship can also change over the course of a campaign.

For my purposes, a useful Force has all four of these qualities:

- It is more powerful than the characters in the arena relevant to its goal, and can affect the situation in ways they cannot easily ignore.
- It has a goal it is trying to achieve.
- It has lines it will and will not cross.
- It has a fingerprint: a recognizable signature in how it acts.

The comparison is specific to the arena where the Force pursues its goal; it does not have to be more powerful than the characters in every way. A mayor may have far greater influence over city policy while being no match for the characters in a fight. A church may have a food network and community trust the characters lack, while depending on them in another arena. A Force's power might come from political authority, money, public trust, specialized knowledge, social reach, supernatural influence, or control of something people need. What matters is that it can make things happen in pursuit of its goal at the scale relevant to the campaign.

A fingerprint is the Force's signature in the way it acts: its characteristic methods, habits, priorities, or way of treating people. I borrow the idea from children's cartoons, where a hero or villain has a signature way of doing things that makes them recognizable—even in disguise. I use a Force's fingerprint to make its actions feel as if they come from that particular actor and belong in the same world. When I decide what the Force does, I let its signature shape the action, rather than merely adding a clue or calling card afterward. The players may then connect separate events, recognize a disguised Force, or learn which fingerprints they trust or fear. Those are valuable effects, but the fingerprint's first job is to make the Force's behavior feel coherent and distinctive. A force can be an individual or a group; I can treat a group as one character for its shared goal while still treating its members as individuals.

The theme helps me choose goals, methods, and fingerprints that matter in this campaign. A Force can bring one pressure to bear; its relationships and collisions with others can bring out another. I do not make Forces into mouthpieces for a moral position.

A prepared fingerprint is provisional. If a different signature emerges in play, I record and use that pattern rather than forcing the original idea into later scenes.

Being a force does not mean being mysterious or hidden. A force may be publicly known and pursue its goals openly, or conceal its identity or intentions. A fingerprint can make a known Force's behavior distinctive, or give the players a way to recognize it when its identity is concealed.

Forces do not have to be villains or even obvious sources of conflict. A church might organize kitchens and food deliveries because it wants to end hunger. A mayor might court voters and redirect city resources because they want to be reelected. A police chief, haunted by the violence of the streets, might want people to feel safe and use the department's authority to pursue that goal. Each can change the situation through the work it does, the people it brings together, and the choices it makes. Their goals may align with the characters', conflict with them, or simply intersect; good intentions do not guarantee agreement, but neither do they make opposition inevitable.

I also create supporting characters. They do not need to meet the criteria for a force. They can connect the characters to forces, show the effects of those forces, or carry a thematic or emotional thread of their own.

As a rule of thumb, I start with three forces. I give them goals that do not directly oppose one another. Their actions may bring them into conflict, but they may also support or complicate one another, or remain unrelated. Their purposes do not need to be opposite sides of the same struggle.

For my purposes, directly opposing goals simplify two forces down to a single force: everything they do interacts. Separate goals give me more possibilities for how their actions might intersect, whether that produces conflict, cooperation, or no immediate connection.

###### When There Are Too Many Forces in Play ######

There is no fixed maximum number of Forces. The problem is not how many people or groups exist in the world, but how many I need to actively track and bring into play at once. A Stage can contain many possible actors while only a few are currently pursuing goals that matter to the characters.

I may have too many active Forces when I can no longer keep their goals, limits, and fingerprints distinct; when I have to force connections just to use them; or when their competing developments crowd out the situations the players are trying to engage with. The players may also be hearing about more actors and conflicts than they can make sense of, while Arcs multiply faster than they can follow. More preparation in that state can leave me with more notes but less confidence about what would plausibly happen next.

When I notice these signs, I do not need to delete Forces from the world. I can let some recede from the foreground and bring them back when the characters' actions or interests make them relevant. A useful check is: if the characters do something unexpected now, can I tell which Forces would notice, care, and act—and why? If too many seem equally urgent, or I cannot distinguish their likely responses, I should narrow my active focus.

###### When There Are Too Few Forces in Play ######

There is no fixed minimum number of Forces. The question is whether enough independent actors are active to make the Stage move and give the characters meaningful situations to affect. Too few may leave one Force carrying more than its goals and limits can support. If the situation has little motion without that Force, or I have to invent pressure from outside it, the Stage may be functioning as a backdrop rather than a system. When an Arc ends, there may also be no other active goal or developing situation to catch the players' interest.

Too few active fingerprints can make the campaign feel repetitive even when the characters' choices technically change events. If different situations keep unfolding through the same methods, priorities, and kinds of consequences, the world seems to answer in the same voice. Players may begin to feel bored, or that their actions do not matter, because the results all feel alike.

When I notice these signs, I can add or activate another Force, or give an existing actor room to pursue an independent goal. I do not need to add more Forces simply to increase the count; I need enough distinct agency and fingerprints for the situation to produce varied, connected developments. A useful check is: if the current Arc ended or the players ignored it, what else in this part of the world would still be changing?

##### The Stage #####

The Stage is the background of the campaign: its props, places, stories, and relationships. It explains why the forces I have chosen are the forces that matter here. It also needs enough life and movement that other forces can emerge. I develop the Stage so its history, relationships, and pressures help the campaign keep raising its thematic question. No place or piece of history has to stand for the theme by itself; together, they give the forces' actions context and give that context meaning.

Most games already have a canon that describes a populated world. That is usually my starting place, not something I need to replace. My Stage describes some portion of that world and adds enough depth that it feels alive.

I map relationships between forces, including alliances, rivalries, obligations, history, and dependencies. I consider how people and local groups view them: who loves a force, who hates it, and who would hate it if they knew its identity. I distinguish what people know from what they believe, including what the forces know or believe about one another. These notes can be light; a sentence or three may be enough to give me something useful.

The Stage and forces develop together. A force gives me reasons to build parts of the Stage, and those parts suggest new forces. Often I begin play with different forces from the ones that originally inspired me because better options emerge during development. Neither exists independently of the other.

In the campaign with the Nephondi High Mage, he was the initial force. I needed a Stage that allowed him to exist and pursue his goal. That led to the spirit beneath the city. Once I had the spirit, I realized I needed guardians. Because the campaign was set in Baton Rouge, that development led to a were-gator tribe becoming another force.

This connected work is where most of my initial development goes. I may produce dozens of ideas for possible forces, but that is a side effect. I only need three to begin.

###### When the Stage Is Not Developed Enough ######

The Stage may not be developed enough when I keep having to invent foundational details during play instead of drawing on what I have established. I may also struggle to picture ordinary life there: not just the campaign's central conflict, but what people do and how the place feels when that conflict is not in the foreground.

Another sign is that I often find myself without an answer to what the players do. I do not need to know their choices or decide outcomes in advance. I need enough context—people, relationships, history, and pressures—to make a grounded next move when they surprise me. If I cannot see what could plausibly follow from their actions, the Stage may need more development.

###### When the Stage Is Overdeveloped ######

I look for two signs that I have developed the Stage too much:

- **I struggle to find what matters in my own material.** The volume of detail makes the Stage harder to use rather than helping me respond.
- **Development delays play.** I keep preparing instead of starting, even though I already understand the situation well enough to run it.

Unused detail is not itself a problem; it gives me possibilities to draw on. Development becomes excessive when it obstructs access to what matters or keeps the game from beginning. Attachment to prepared material is a different problem: I can resist changing or leaving out details even in a small Stage.

##### When the Stage Is Ready #####

I use four criteria to decide when I have developed the Stage enough:

1. **I am bored with working on it.** I have fiddled and played with it enough that I do not want to keep doing that.
2. **I cannot think of another addition that is both important and interesting for the characters.** Just because something might never be used is no excuse for it to be boring.
3. **It makes sense.** I can understand why everything is there and how each piece affects the others.
4. **I can envision a populated world emerging from it.** It feels like a living portion of the setting, not just a collection of isolated ideas.

The fourth criterion is difficult to explain, especially when the game's existing setting already supplies a populated world. I am not trying to create every person in it. I want the part I have developed to add depth and feel alive within that world.

#### What I Deliberately Leave Undecided ####

Most of what I create for the Stage never appears directly in play. That is useful: it gives me possibilities to draw on when surprised, without turning preparation into a list of things the characters must encounter. I leave their decisions, the sequence of events, and the ending open.

##### Arcs and Stories #####

I use "Arc" and "Story" interchangeably. A collision starts an Arc: the events that fall out of that collision belong to the same narrative device. That device can end, even while the campaign continues.

Players may talk about the Forces, but when choosing what to pursue, they engage with Arcs: the situations and developing stories that grow from the Forces' actions. Forces are the engine that creates those situations; the Arc is the main unit of player engagement. I prepare Forces so they can produce Arcs the players want to engage with.

An Arc ends in one of two ways:

- The players stop engaging with it.
- Its fallout reaches a natural conclusion based on character actions.

A natural ending gives the table a sense of having completed something. In rulesets that award experience for completing stories or similar milestones, it also provides a natural point to gain XP.

I suggest having three Arcs in play, introducing them across three sessions rather than starting everything at once. That staggered start lets complexity grow and gives the campaign a sense of depth. It is a rule of thumb, not a schedule I protect from play. I am willing to change it, or anything else, when play calls for that.

The important distinction is that the three Arcs begin with three different collisions involving three different pairs of goals. They are not simply three threads from one collision. As another rule of thumb, I involve no more than two forces in each collision.

The same forces can participate in different Arcs. It is possible for the same pair of forces to collide over different pairs of goals, but I do not suggest that as the starting arrangement.

##### Preparing a Collision #####

Before an Arc starts, I know:

- The two forces involved.
- The goals driving their actions.
- What caused the conflict.
- The combatants.

For the first combat of the game, I also know where it takes place and whether I intend it to be a victory or a defeat for the characters. Otherwise, the location remains undecided. Everything else is open.

For example, consider these three forces:

- **Force A** wants to become mayor.
- **Force B** wants to bring all crime in the city under its control.
- **Force C** wants to remove its biggest business competitor from the city.

None of those goals directly opposes another. The collisions come from what the forces do to pursue them:

1. **A and C collide over a strike.** C has caused a strike, and A uses local authorities to break it up to gain votes in the upcoming election.
2. **B and C collide over a drive-by.** C's beefed-up private security stops a drive-by near its business that would have eliminated a gang leader.
3. **A and B collide through public violence.** A gang leader's daughter works for A. B uses bribed authorities to take out that leader with lethal force at a conference for A.

These can start three distinct Arcs using only three forces.

The conference is an example of where the event might happen, not a place I need to push the characters toward. Before that session, I only need to know that B will oppose A through violence in a public space because the gang leader's daughter works for A. I choose the public space based on where the characters go.

That is how I leave later collisions flexible enough to weave into character actions. I prepare the conflict, not the characters' route to it.

#### How Characters Connect to the Game ####

Usually, I do most of this development after the table has formed but before we meet to make characters. Character creation then gives me details to backfill into the Stage.

There is no fixed amount of information I give the players before character creation. It depends on the theme and the particular game. Knowing the theme, Stage, initial forces, and opening collision gives me material to decide what the players should know and what their characters should know.

I share a detail when it serves one or more of these purposes:

1. It prevents surprise about the type of game being run.
2. It guides players toward characters who fit the Stage and chosen theme.
3. It helps explain the opening combat afterward.

I keep those details as brief as possible, and no briefer. I want enough information for players to make fitting characters and understand the kind of game they are joining, without making them sit through unnecessary opening rhetoric. Content expectations and safety boundaries still need to be established; reducing exposition does not replace that conversation.

Sometimes I do not know the inciting incident until the characters are made. I have even held off on creating the Stage and forces until then. I do not recommend that unless the GM and players are experienced and have played many games together.

#### Giving Players Something Worth Engaging With ####

##### The Opening Collision #####

I always start the game with combat arising from a collision of forces. The characters do not have to fight the forces directly; they can be caught in the fallout of their actions.

Most games have their most developed rules in combat. Starting there lets the players try their new characters using the part of the game the rules support most heavily. It also focuses the table immediately. I have never had an opening combat fail to engage the players; it was the way I found to begin a campaign with everyone interested.

But the opening combat is the dreaded railroad. The characters must already have made some decision to be in a place where the combat can happen. I am making that starting decision for them, so I do not want to build too much around it. This prepared frame is useful only for the first few moments of the first session; once play is underway, I follow the players' choices rather than treating the opening as a route the campaign must continue to follow.

My rule is: **The decision must be something the players can accept that their characters did before the game started.**

If they cannot accept that premise, I have lost their engagement before combat begins. Preparing an opening situation is not permission to assign them choices that do not fit their characters.

##### A Non-Lethal First Fight #####

As a rule of thumb, the opening combat needs to be guaranteed non-lethal. This is the players' first chance to use their characters, and they are going to assume they will win. Winning does not have to happen, but losing should not mean losing those new characters.

I ensure this through the encounter and its consequences rather than announcing the guarantee beforehand. My goal is to reduce opening rhetoric; the players do not need an explanation of this preparation. They need to see the consequences afterward.

When I intend the opening to be a victory, I make the combat well below the characters' abilities: a sure win. When I intend it to be a loss, the opposition's objective is to capture or drive them away, and the enemies do not use lethal combat techniques.

This is a specific decision about the first fight, not a predetermined outcome for the Arc. The characters' responses and the events that follow remain open.

##### When Combat Ends in Failure #####

The opening fight is a special case, but the principle applies to combat more broadly: **failure in combat should always lead to a more interesting situation.** I take this subrule from *Fate Core*. It applies to losing a combat, not to an individual failed roll.

A character's death can be the right outcome, but it is not automatically the most interesting one. Capture, for example, may give the characters new problems and choices to face. I look for a loss that changes the situation in a way the table can engage with, rather than defaulting to death.

##### Letting Questions Bring Out the Background #####

Once the combat is over, the players start asking questions. Now I can give them the opening explanation because they are seeking it instead of waiting for me to finish talking.

In one campaign, every character had a police officer as a contact. That connection existed before the fight, but afterward I explained that the characters were there because the contact had asked them to look into something. I gave everyone a free advantage because I knew what the opening needed.

The connection made the starting decision plausible for the characters. The combat gave the players something immediate to do. Their questions then gave me a way to explain the situation when they wanted to understand it.

#### Trying This Approach ####

Choose a theme, then develop a Stage and Forces whose connections can generate distinct collisions. Prepare enough for a usable starting situation, including an opening the players can accept, but leave later locations and outcomes open. Share the context players need to make fitting characters, then use their ideas to enrich the Stage.

### 6. Preparing for Play ###

#### What I Prepare and Why ####

Preparing a campaign and preparing for a session are different kinds of work. Before play begins, I spend about 70% of my initial preparation building the Stage and about 20% building the forces. That work gives me an understanding of the world and the people or groups acting in it. It is not a schedule of events for the characters to follow.

Between sessions, I prepare much less. I review what the characters changed and prepare relevant fallout, using the process in Chapter 10 to keep it thematic and grounded in the established situation.

I prepare the things the characters will need to spend effort on. If there is a clue for them to pursue, I prepare it. If there are combatants for them to defeat, I prepare them. If there is a key character they may try to build a relationship with, I prepare that character. The players decide what to do with these things and what comes of their efforts.

#### What My Notes Look Like ####

People need to find the level of detail and format that work best for them. I keep my notes brief, and I use Markdown for everything. I usually give each important thing its own short file. I try to keep a force to no more than two screens of information, and hope to use less.

The notes should be short enough to use and detailed enough to help me make decisions. I do not need to write down every possibility.

##### Improvising Without Looking Unprepared #####

Many GMs, especially new ones, worry that improvising will make them look unprepared. Knowing the Stage, forces, and their relationships gives you something solid to work from: you can connect a new detail to what is already true or make sense of a pattern as it emerges. Those connections can create a shared sense of wonder without requiring you to have planned them in advance.

#### When Preparation Is Sufficient ####

A session is ready when I understand the relevant fallout and have prepared the material characters may need to work for: clues, combatants, or key NPCs. That is a stopping point for preparation, not a prediction of what the session will contain.

#### An Annotated Example of My Session Prep ####

Here is one way I might prepare a session: note the fallout, identify useful open questions, and prepare material the characters may spend effort on.

##### Example: After the warehouse attack #####

The last session ended with the characters exposing a forged permit at the River Market and forcing a confrontation with the guild's private enforcers. The market is furious, frightened, and eager to find someone to blame. The characters are now the obvious target.

```text
Session Prep: River Market

Fallout
- The warehouse fire is still smoldering; people are scared, angry, and looking for a scapegoat.
- The guild is suppressing rumors, but a few workers are willing to talk if the characters can promise safety.
- The spirit beneath the city is stirring and leaving traces in the old drains beneath the market.

Things that require effort
- Clue: a ledger page showing payment to a councilor tied to the guild.
- Clue: a half-burned note reading "salt the shrine before sunrise."
- Combatants: four masked enforcers, two dock thugs, one guild fixer.
- Key NPC: Ilya Moss, a broker who wants the characters to keep the market quiet while she figures out what the guild is hiding.

Open questions
- Does the councilor know what the guild is doing, or is the guild using him?
- Is the spirit reacting to the characters, or just to the disturbances above it?
- What happens if the characters expose the ledger before they can verify it?
```

The notes identify pressure points: an unstable market, people willing to talk, clues to follow, enemies to face, and a broker with leverage and a reason to negotiate.

##### Why This Works #####

The open questions show what is uncertain and what can wait. The players might pursue the shrine, negotiate with Ilya, or attack the enforcers; each choice changes the situation differently. These notes help me respond without deciding which path they take.

### 7. My Basic Loop at the Table ###

#### The Loop ####

At the table, I keep returning to a simple loop: I present what is happening, find out what the players want to do, decide what needs resolution, establish what changes, and give the situation back to them. This is not a script or a set of steps I have to perform mechanically. It is a way to keep play responsive: the players can act on what they see, and the world can change in response.

#### Present What Is Happening ####

I describe the part of the situation the characters can perceive and act on. That might be what a person is doing, what has changed because of an earlier action, or the immediate effects of a force pursuing its goal. I give enough information for the players to understand what their characters could reasonably notice, but I do not need to explain the whole Stage or every cause behind the moment.

If the characters have questions, I answer from what they know, what they can discover, and what is actually true in the world. Sometimes the players' questions are the best cue for what background to explain. I want them to learn about the situation because they are interested in it, not because I have stopped play to deliver everything I prepared.

#### Find Out What the Players Want to Do ####

I let the players decide what their characters attempt. If I am unsure what a player means, I ask what the character is trying to accomplish or how they intend to approach it. That gives me a better basis for deciding what happens.

#### Decide What Needs Resolution ####

Once I understand the intention, I decide whether anything needs to be resolved. Some actions are clear from the situation and need no roll or extended discussion. When the outcome is uncertain, I ask whether failure would make the current story more interesting; I roll only if it would. Otherwise, I resolve the action without a roll. I can use a ruling or talk through the situation with the players when that helps. How I choose between these approaches, and how I handle a difficult ruling, belongs to the next chapter.

#### Establish What Changes ####

I first ask, “What is the most interesting outcome that can happen within the campaign's theme?” Then I work out how it can grow from the action and the situation already established: the Stage, the Forces and their goals and limits, and the relationships in play. If I cannot find a grounded way for that outcome to happen, I look for another thematic possibility rather than forcing it. Theme leads what I consider; the established situation helps me make the outcome belong. Chapter 10 covers how to develop and reveal that fallout.

#### Give the Situation Back to the Players ####

I make the change visible, then return the focus to the players. They need to see enough of what happened to choose what their characters do next. That may mean showing the immediate result, describing a reaction, or revealing a clue to a larger problem. I do not need to explain every implication at once; the players can investigate, ask questions, or move in another direction.

Their next choice begins the loop again. The forces react to what the characters have changed, and the world develops from the actions at the table. I use the loop to keep play moving while leaving the outcome open.

### 8. Making Decisions in the Moment ###

#### Choosing How to Resolve Something ####

When a character tries something, I first decide whether the outcome needs resolving at all. If it is clear from the situation, I say what happens and keep play moving. If it is uncertain and matters, I choose how to resolve it: use the rules, make a ruling, or talk it through with the players. I choose the approach that helps us understand what happens without letting the process get in the way of the game.

##### The Rule of Interesting #####

Before I roll, I ask whether failure would make the current story more interesting. **Only roll the dice when failure will cause the current story to be more interesting.** I call this the Rule of Interesting. I learned the idea from the original *7th Sea*, though it did not call it that; this wording is mine. If failure would not make the story more interesting, I resolve the action without a roll. Uncertainty alone is not a reason to roll.

This is different from asking what the most interesting outcome within the theme might be. That question helps me decide what happens; the Rule of Interesting helps me decide whether to roll.

Rules are useful tools, not authorities that outrank the people playing. If a rule supports the moment, I use it. If I do not know the rule, I let the player attempt the action for now and tell them I will check it for future sessions. If the dice or system are getting in the way of the table's fun, I set them aside and play make-believe instead.

#### Handling Uncertainty and Missing Information ####

I do not need to know everything before making a decision. I use what is established: the Stage, the forces and their goals and limits, what the characters know, and what has already happened. If something important is unclear, I can ask the players what they mean, talk through the uncertainty, or make a provisional ruling so play can continue. If several answers fit, I choose the one that best fits the established situation. I can correct a mistaken rule or fact going forward without erasing what already happened.

#### Making Rulings Players Can Understand ####

I try to make rulings in terms of the character and the situation, and to say enough that the players understand what I am deciding. I do not need to turn every call into a long debate. My usual framework is:

1. **I do not know the rule:** The player can do it for now. I will look up the rule before a future session.
2. **The character probably cannot do it, but the attempt is plausible:** I may allow it with a slight increase in difficulty.
3. **The action is too outlandish for the character:** I use “No, but.” I say no to that specific action, then help the player find another way to pursue the character's goal.

If there is a conflict about a rule or ruling, I bring it to a table vote and move on. Safety is different: any player can veto content without explanation, and that veto is not put to a vote.

#### Correcting a Rules Call Without Rewriting the Past ####

If I later learn that a ruling was wrong, I do not take back what already happened or erase a past success to match the rulebook. I explain the correction and apply the rule consistently going forward; the earlier event remains part of the game, but does not necessarily set a precedent.

#### Correcting a Decision That Did Not Work ####

If a decision makes play less fun, undermines a character, or creates a problem I did not intend, I acknowledge it, explain what I am changing, and move forward with a clearer understanding.

Safety is the exception to preserving past events: when someone raises a concern, I erase the offending action and its direct consequences. I make a note without asking for an explanation, then help the affected player find another way forward if the action was theirs.

### 9. Keeping Play Moving ###

#### Recognizing What Deserves Attention ####

I notice what the players ask about and pursue, but a thread losing attention is different from a player losing interest in the game. If I am concerned about someone's engagement—for example, if they start spending time on their phone—I talk with them privately after the session rather than treating it as a story problem. If someone says they dislike a thread, I take that seriously.

#### Giving Players Room Without Losing Momentum ####

I do not try to maintain momentum by filling every pause or pushing the players toward a decision. I let them think, talk, ask questions, and decide what matters to their characters. Awkward silence can be useful. It gives a player space to work out what they want to do, and I may remind the rest of the table to let that space exist rather than rushing to fill it.

Momentum comes from the situation changing in response to the players, not from hurrying them.

#### Sharing Attention Among Players ####

I avoid asking the table a broad question like, “What are you all doing now?” Instead, I address each player through their character. After a conflict, for example, I might ask, “What is Luna thinking? What is your next priority?” This gives each player a direct opening to contribute without requiring them to compete for space in a group conversation.

After I have heard from each player, I ask the table to make a plan together. I give them a few moments to talk, then go around and check in with each player again, still using their character's name. The group has room to collaborate, while each person still gets a chance to say what their character wants.

I do not have a complete formula for sharing attention. It is nuanced and changes with the people and situation at the table. This is one technique I use to make sure that everyone has an invitation to take part.

#### Handling Hesitation and Unexpected Choices ####

When players make an unexpected choice, I follow it rather than steering them back toward what I expected. Their choice changes the situation; I use what I know about the Stage and forces to respond.

#### Knowing When to Move On ####

When players move on from a thread, I stop foregrounding it rather than pushing it back into play. Its consequences may remain in the world; the distinction between an unresolved thread and a completed Arc matters when considering the campaign as a whole (see Chapter 12).

### 10. Bringing the World to Life ###

#### Deciding What to Describe ####

I try to give at least two concrete details for each scene and for every NPC or group of NPCs. I describe enough of the background for people to understand the situation, then let their minds fill in the rest. The details do not need to be elaborate. They need to give the players something specific to picture and act on.

The theme helps me decide which details to foreground and how to frame them. Two scenes can contain the same facts but feel different depending on what the description emphasizes.

For example:

> As you wait in the dimly lit parking lot of a medium-sized church, three rough-looking men ride up on Harley-Davidson motorcycles. They are the remaining heads of the local gangs, and they look pissed.

That is the whole lead-up description. The parking lot and church establish the scene; the men, their motorcycles, and their anger make the arrival concrete. The players know who has arrived and what kind of moment this is without needing a long description of the lot, the building, or each man's appearance. I give them enough to imagine the scene, then leave space for their own picture of it.

#### Portraying People and Their Motivations ####

I want NPCs to feel like people with reasons for what they do, not pieces I move around to deliver information or serve a plot. Every NPC has goals. Those goals are often immediate and obvious, and they govern the NPC's actions and interactions with the characters.

An NPC can still serve a purpose in the campaign. In one game, I had a woman who was meant to give the players information and demonstrate one of the forces' power. She was also trying to save her son, who was a prisoner of war. If she succeeded, he would live free; if she failed, he would remain a POW. That goal shaped every interaction she had with the characters. Her campaign role did not replace her own reason to act.

NPCs also have emotions. Most of the time, these are not explosive or theatrical, but they still affect how people respond. If the characters insult an NPC, that person might act injured or self-righteous, depending on who they are and what they want. The goal gives the interaction direction; the emotion gives it a human texture.

In combat, I make sure at least one NPC has a name and is called by it. A name gives the fight weight and draws attention to the fact that these are people. If I have the time and inspiration while preparing, I name all the combatants.

#### Responding to What the Characters Do ####

The characters' significant actions change the situation. My first question is, “What is the most interesting outcome that can happen within the campaign's theme?” I start there, rather than first listing likely consequences and only afterward looking for a thematic one. Then I work out how that outcome can grow from what the characters did and from the Stage, Forces, goals, limits, and relationships already in play. If I cannot find a grounded way for it to happen, I reconsider the outcome rather than forcing it into the situation.

After that, I ask what else follows. I expect a significant act to have at least two consequences: one often immediate, another perhaps several sessions later. These further effects should grow from the same changed situation, not become a quota of extra threads to maintain. Consequences can be beneficial, harmful, or mixed; they should deepen the situation, not punish the players or erase their success. The thematic outcome gives the fallout its focus, while the established world gives it a way to happen.

Suppose the campaign asks, “Can a community become safe without reproducing violence?” If the characters kill the head of a local gang, one interesting outcome is that people the leader hurt thank them and offer to help make the neighborhood safer, while removing the leader destabilizes the underground power structure and increases gang violence. That puts the question back into play through a real change: the characters have helped people, and the power vacuum creates a new pressure around what safety will mean. Both results grow from the same act; neither erases what the characters accomplished or dictates what they should do next.

#### Making Consequences Visible ####

I want the players to encounter the effects of their choices, even when those effects are not immediately obvious. Consequences can show up in changed circumstances, other people's behavior, or details of ordinary life—not only through an NPC explaining what the characters caused.

In the earlier campaign that inspired the example in Chapter 14, the characters were trying to find the cause of a massacre that had happened twenty years earlier. The Mokolé were openly buying land, and their goals collided with the Vampires' interests, setting off a real-estate war. Land prices soared and housing costs rose so sharply that the news began reporting on apartments where large numbers of people were sharing rooms.

That kind of ripple makes the characters important even if the world does not know why things are happening. A news report can reveal the larger effect without explaining every link in the chain. In another game, stopping an evil corporation meant that its factory site eventually became a park. Fallout can be a lasting improvement, not just a new problem.

#### Keeping the World Coherent as It Changes ####

Let consequences grow from the established situation. Effects may be indirect or take time to appear; show what changed and let the players discover its connection if they investigate.
